A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CodePDE and its five-PDE, 16-LLM study. The text, equations, figures, tables and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching relocated analyses and reformatted code.

before.justification: Sections 5 and the appendices report original evaluations of generated solvers, including accuracy, debugging success, convergence, execution time and numerical-scheme choices.

after.justification: V2 retains these original evaluations and adds component ablations, token-usage analysis and an experiment using expert hints for reaction–diffusion solver generation.

M1.justification: The five-step CodePDE pipeline, standard prompts and existing case-study solver implementations remain unchanged. Appendix D adds a limited expert-guided variant that supplies operator-splitting advice and the analytical reaction update in the generation prompt.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate Advection, Burgers, Reaction-Diffusion, Compressible Navier-Stokes and Darcy Flow using PDEBench and FNO data with unchanged PDE specifications. The added comparisons, ablations and hint experiment use these existing tasks.

E2.justification: Tables 1, 3 and 4 add Dedalus and PyPDE comparisons on four PDE families and remove the Central Finite Diff. result rows. The neural baselines, FunSearch and AIDE remain. Human Expert is renamed Reference Numerical Solvers; the appendix's FunSearch-PDE and AIDE-PDE labels do not identify new comparators.

E3.justification: Table 2 replaces the best-LLM-per-method summary with a common Claude-3.7-sonnet comparison and adds cumulative component-removal controls. V2 also reports convergence failures alongside convergence orders, measures output-token usage and introduces a best-of-32 hint/no-hint experiment. These substantially extend the evaluation design; they do not establish that the retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V2 adds explicit ablations of refinement, sampling and debugging, extends convergence analysis to failures, and tests whether expert guidance mitigates the reaction–diffusion failure mode. Appendix A.7 adds inference-cost analysis. Existing execution-time and library-usage analyses are retained in the appendix rather than removed.

E5.justification: Both versions disclose 32 i.i.d. generated solvers per model/problem for debugging statistics and retain the same sampling budgets. Neither reports repeated-experiment uncertainty, confidence intervals or significance tests. The added token averages do not introduce a new uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: The original CodePDE and full FunSearch/AIDE accuracy rows are retained, but v2 adds software-baseline, ablation, token-use and hint results. Table 10 reports nRMSE 1.69e-3 with hints versus 1.44e-1 without hints, with runtime increasing from 191.61 to 1221.57 seconds. Revised convergence distributions include a 60.5% CNS failure rate. Numerical summaries also change, including Table 4's reference geometric mean from 3.13e-3 to 2.38e-3.

T1.justification: The PDE definitions, nRMSE formula and mathematical convergence criterion remain equivalent. No new theorem, proof or derivation is introduced. The analytical reaction update supplied in the new hint already appears in v1's reference-solver code.

C1.justification: V2 replaces the abstract and introduction's broad human-level or superhuman claims with performance relative to specific numerical reference solvers and software. The four-of-five result remains in Section 5.1 with this narrower comparator. The abstract and conclusion newly emphasize reliability-versus-sophistication trade-offs and principles for designing PDE-solving agents.

C2.justification: V2 interprets agent results as evidence that shared debugging, refinement and scaling capabilities matter more than the search strategy, replacing v1's emphasis on CodePDE superiority. It adds the reliability/sophistication interpretation, discusses expert hints as mitigation, and substantially expands trust conditions and neural-solver comparison qualifications in Appendix E.

D1.justification: V2 newly documents 50 development instances separate from 100 test instances per family, 1200/2400-second timeouts, reference-solver schemes, refinement-feedback formatting, FunSearch's 12-plus-20 iteration allocation and o3/o4-mini classification of solver schemes. It also adds evaluation-data access information and reports Terminal Bench/Harbor integration. These are disclosures, not evidence that the corresponding retained settings changed.

R1.justification: V2 adds numerical-software references such as Dedalus, py-pde and Basix, along with additional neural-PDE and scientific-agent literature, while removing some earlier citations such as SciCode. The three-part related-work organization and first-framework positioning remain, with the closing comparison reframed around systematic capability evaluation.

P1.justification: The abstract, contribution narrative and conclusion are substantially rewritten. Results subsections gain explicit takeaways, convergence receives a dedicated treatment, and execution-time and library discussions move to Appendix A. Implementation documentation is reorganized, and new discussion and broader-impact appendices replace much of the earlier future-directions framing.

P2.justification: V2 adopts a different journal layout, removes v1's introductory radial comparison plot, restructures Table 2 and redraws convergence displays with failure categories and additional models. It adds three token-usage figures, reference-solver tables and the hint-results table, while relocating existing runtime and library figures into the appendix.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially improves the evidential basis and calibration of the paper. Common-backbone comparisons and component ablations clarify the sources of performance, while explicit convergence failures expose reliability limitations hidden by v1's order-only plots. Software baselines, documented feedback/test separation and narrower reference-solver claims address important comparison and reproducibility weaknesses. The hint experiment adds useful diagnostic evidence, with its dependence on expert input and increased runtime visible in Table 10.
